title: Venom / Shockwave
label: Slimzos
tracklist_note: Two tracks, 'Venom' and 'Shockwave'. Plastician's Bandcamp says 'Shockwave' was produced in 2001 and was his first release.

sound_descriptions.text: Plastician describes 'Venom' as an '8-bar' grime track, made in FruityLoops when he had little production experience.
Wikipedia describes his early work as a 'grimy take on the instrumental sound' from the darker side of UK garage (artist-level, not track-specific).

context.text: Released on Slimzos, the imprint of Rinse FM DJ Slimzee; Plasticman's first 12".
Plastician sent early tracks to Slimzee on CD via the Rhythm Division shop; Slimzee signed two of them to Slimzos and played them.
Plasticman was born and based in Croydon (Thornton Heath), South London.
Reissued digitally on 'Plasticman Remastered (Deluxe Edition)', 14 July 2014.

uncertainty: No catalogue number found. The track pairing 'Venom / Shockwave' and 'early 2002' come from Wikipedia only; Bandcamp confirms Shockwave on Slimzos in 2002. Discogs blocked, so not cross-checked.

title: Hard Graft
artist: Plasticman (sleeve credit given by the dealer listing as 'Mark One Vs. Plasticman')
label: Contagious Recordings
format: 12" vinyl, 45 rpm, white label with sticker
tracklist_note: A: Plasticman – Hard Graft (5:05); B: Hard Graft (Mark One Remix) (4:26).

context.text: Plastician called it his third release, from about 2002–03, and opened his 2004 Red Bull Music Academy lecture with it.
Wikipedia links 'Hard Graft' to DJ Hatcha's support and to Plasticman's 2003 releases through Ammunition Promotions imprints.
A commenter on k-punk's 2004 post called 'Hard Graft' the best track they had heard in ages (reader comment, not the author).

relationships.other: Hard Graft (Mark One Remix), on the B-side of the same 12"

uncertainty: Label conflict: the dealer listing (which cites Discogs release r22630064) says Contagious Recordings, CONTAGIOUS-004, April 2003. Wikipedia instead ties 'Hard Graft' to 2003 releases on Soulja and ROAD, Ammunition Promotions imprints. Contagious may be a third imprint, or there may be more than one pressing; this is unresolved. RBMA credits the track as 'Mark One vs. Plasticman'. No published description of the sound was found. Note: the 'Industrial Graft' on the Rephlex 'Grime' comp is a different title and was not assumed to be the same track.

title: Fight / Fight (Plasticman Remix)
label: Terrorhythm Recordings
tracklist_note: Original plus Plasticman remix. First release on Plasticman's Terrorhythm label.
discogs_url: https://www.discogs.com/release/307460-Mark-One-Fight (found in search; page could not be opened)

context.text: Terrorhythm was founded in 2002 by Plastician; TERR001 was Mark One's 'Fight' with a Plasticman remix.
In 2003 Mark One held a weekly Rinse FM slot alongside Plastician and Virus Syndicate.
Mark One later recorded as MRK1; the MRK1 article lists 'Fight' as a 2003 single on 'Terro Rhythm'.
Plastician describes 'Fight' as a collaboration with Mark One on Terrorhythm.

relationships.other: Fight (Plasticman Remix), on the same release

uncertainty: No published description of the sound was found. The format ('12"') is inferred from Terrorhythm being a vinyl label and from the A/B remix pairing; Discogs could not be opened to confirm it. The MRK1 article was read on an mdwiki.org mirror of Wikipedia.

title: Cha EP (The Cha E.P.)
label: Terrorhythm Recordings
tracklist_note: Plastician describes it as a three-track EP; only 'Cha' could be confirmed by name.
discogs_url: https://www.discogs.com/release/320570-Plasticman-Cha-EP (found in search; page could not be opened; master: https://www.discogs.com/master/529337-Plasticman-Cha-EP)

sound_descriptions.text: FACT calls 'Cha' a classic from the period when grime and dubstep were not yet separate (genre placement only, no sonic detail).
In his 2004 lecture Plastician described his production generally: FruityLoops, WAV basslines, an 808-style kit, 'fat and warm' bass, around 140 bpm (not specific to 'Cha').

context.text: Plastician called 'Cha' 'quite big' and recalled hearing electro DJs play it at a Rebel Bass night.
Plastician says it was the first release he distributed himself, after starting his own label.
Bandcamp: 'Produced in 2002, originally released on Terrorhythm as part of The Cha E.P. released in 2004.'

uncertainty: Release year: Wikipedia and Bandcamp both say 2004. The other tracks on the EP were not confirmed because Discogs could not be opened. There is no detailed published description of the sound of the original.

title: Grime
label: Rephlex
format: Compilation: CD (Village Voice) and vinyl ('triple-pack LP' per Plastician; k-punk calls it an LP)
release_date: 2004 (gridface review dated 23 May 2004; Plastician places it around early 2004)
tracklist_note: About four tracks per artist. Named tracks: Mark One 'Stargate 92', 'Raindance', 'Interference'; Plasticman 'Pump up the Jam' (k-punk) / 'Camel Ride' or 'Camel Aide' / 'Industrial Graft' / 'The Music'; Slaughter Mob 'Dub Weapon', 'Creeky Door'. Titles differ slightly between reviews.

sound_descriptions.text: k-punk: no MCs; a South London grime with the 'silver impersonality and sleekness of stainless steel'.
Mark One's 'Stargate 92': menacing beats with early-1990s synths and MC grunts; 'Raindance' sets repeated female vocal samples over dark, repetitive bass.
Plasticman's 'Industrial Graft' sounds slowed down and heavy, mechanical and oppressive; 'Camel Ride' has warbling samples at high bpm.
Slaughter Mob: Jamaican-accented vocals, deep rolling bass, and horror effects (creaking doors, owl hoots) over bleep, break and bass.

context.text: Rephlex's Grant Wilson-Claridge heard Plastician at FWD>> (Plastic People) and asked him for beats; Plastician calls it 'the first grime CD'.
Rephlex used the line 'Grime. Sublow. Dubstep... It's Music' in 2004 (as quoted by a record shop).
Plastician himself said it 'was kind of grime, but it wasn't specifically'.
A Vice 'Beats' columnist questioned whether Rephlex understood grime, given the tracklisting.
Followed by 'Grime 2' (CAT 160), which Plastician said was technically dubstep.

relationships.other: Technotronic – 'Pump Up the Jam' (Plasticman's track reworks it, per k-punk)

uncertainty: Wikipedia gives the catalogue number CAT 156 but no date. The track titles differ between reviews ('Camel Aide'/'Camel Ride'), and k-punk's 'Pump up the Jam' may be the 'Pump' named in the brief. The Vice 'Beats' column remark comes from https://www.vice.com/en/article/beats-v11n4/. This is a compilation and arguably closer to proto-dubstep; register it as a crossover document.

title: One Way
label: Planet Mu
tracklist_note: Mostly instrumental, with three tracks featuring Virus Syndicate MCs (JSD on 'Stand Up', MC Goldfinger on 'Ready for It', Nika D on 'Contagious Rhymin''). Other tracks named: 'Bang Bang Boy', 'Call Back', 'Blow', 'Bring the Law'.

sound_descriptions.text: Planet Mu: grime fused with hip hop, electro and drum and bass, with 'menacing bass' and 'spacey production'.
Igloo: mostly instrumental, 'trudging and dark'; 'Bang Bang Boy' is hard and noisy and less minimal than typical grime.
Daily Lobo: Wu-Tang-style strings and dub-like instrumentals; 'Bang Bang Boy' sets gun samples over a wobbly dub bass.

context.text: Igloo calls it one of the first full-length grime albums to get wide attention outside the UK, and Planet Mu's first major grime release.
Mark One was linked with Manchester's Virus Syndicate, who supplied much of the album's vocals.
Mark One was a former drum and bass DJ (Daily Lobo).

uncertainty: Mark One's own home city was not confirmed (Virus Syndicate are from Manchester). The release date comes from Planet Mu's own listing. Format comes from the Igloo page title.

title: Cock Back
artist: Nasty Crew (Hitman Hyper and D Double E, with Crazy Titch and Riko Dan)
label: Aftershock
tracklist_note: Vocal record over a Terror Danjah beat; later versions are listed under relationships.

sound_descriptions.text: Samples the film 'Shottas'.
Terror Danjah's producer tag, a distorted 'gremlin' laugh from a drum and bass sample CD, is part of his sound (artist-level, not confirmed on this track).

context.text: It was the 'Power Play' on Deja Vu FM and topped the sales chart at Rhythm Division; Terror Danjah claimed sales of about 10,000.
Nasty Crew was founded in Plaistow, with members mainly from Newham, East London; Terror Danjah is from Forest Gate.
Aftershock was co-founded in late 2002 by Terror Danjah and Flash as a vinyl-only label, with printed colour labels from its second release.

relationships.other: Cock Back (East Co. Version), 2004, on 'Box Bloody Fresh', featuring Jookie Mundo and Demon
Cock Back V1.2, featuring Riko Dan and Bruza, on 'Run the Road' (679 Recordings, 24 January 2005)

uncertainty: The artist credit varies: the Nasty Crew article gives Hitman Hyper and D Double E with guests Crazy Titch and Riko Dan, while the Aftershock article says 'Nasty Crew feat. Titch and Riko Dan'. The Run the Road article credits 'Terror Danjah featuring Riko, Bruza, D Double E and Hyper' (the V1.2 version). No catalogue number was found.

title: Industry Standard EP
label: Aftershock
format: EP (vinyl; Aftershock was vinyl-only at the time)
tracklist_note: Fully instrumental; includes 'Creepy Crawler'. A separate later 'Industry Standard Trilogy EP' (Lifesaver / Radar / Stiff / Freak Show VIP) exists and should not be confused with it.

sound_descriptions.text: 'Creepy Crawler' has low horns 'like a Blaxploitation soundtrack' and G-funk synth squiggles.
His beats in general: 'crunchy eight-bit noises' around G-funk-style melodies, intricate syncopation, and a distorted 'gremlin' laugh tag.

context.text: Wikipedia describes it as Terror Danjah's breakthrough instrumental EP on Aftershock.
The blog says it stood out among the dozens of 12"s reaching London record shops at the time.

relationships.other: Wiley – 'Take Chances' (XL Recordings, 2004, B-side to 'Pies'), a vocal version of 'Creepy Crawler'
Wiley and Breeze over 'Creepy Crawler' on the Sidewinder Bonus CD, mixed by Logan Sama

uncertainty: The full tracklist, catalogue number and month are unknown, and the format is not stated directly. The MusicBrainz mirror (mb.videolan.org) shows a 12" 'Industry Standard Trilogy EP' (Discogs 708293) with different tracks and no date; it was not used for this entry. The slowmotion.blog source is a personal blog.

title: War
label: White label
tracklist_note: Collected on the Sneaker Social Club compilation 'Sublow' (SNKRLP015), which covers beats from 1999 to 2005.

sound_descriptions.text: Complex: 'synth-rattling, horn-blasting'.
Digi-dub style horns (also on 'Battle'); Cash's sound runs at about 140 bpm with heavy, exaggerated bass and hard drums.
Rubadub: drums 'hard as nails', bass 'tuned for maximum rave damage' (compilation-level).

context.text: Jon E Cash gave Slimzee the dub at a Sidewinder rave; Slimzee played it on Rinse twice each Sunday, reportedly the only DJ with it for two years before release.
Jon E Cash, a West London artist and founding member of the Black Ops crew, is credited with inventing sublow, a West London pocket of grime.
He described his early white labels to Nicky Blackmarket and J Da Flex as 'between garage and hip-hop'; the sublow name came from this sound.
Last.fm lists 'War' among the top Black Ops productions.

relationships.other: Novelist vocal over Jon E Cash's 'War' (2015)

uncertainty: The release year depends on Complex's 'released on white label back in '03'. Boiler Room's 'two years before its release' suggests the dub circulated from about 2001. No label or catalogue number was found, and Discogs was blocked. Sources on sublow are mainly record-shop copy for the reissue.

title: What
label: Dump Valve
tracklist_note: Reissued about 2014 as a limited, hand-numbered 12" in the Rinse 20th-anniversary series, backed with Wizzbit (Geeneus alias) 'Jam Hot'.

sound_descriptions.text: Frieze: oriental chimes reminiscent of Ryuichi Sakamoto over a dense, smog-thick bass.
Complex: a 'warping digital flute' from the Plugsound software series.

context.text: Frieze calls it Dump Valve's definitive release and says it strongly influenced South London dubstep.
Dump Valve was DJ Target's East London label, set up in 2001 and associated with Pay As U Go and Rinse FM.
Slimzee names 'What' among the defining tracks of early grime.

relationships.other: Digital Mystikz – 'Misty Winter' (2006), which frieze calls almost a remix of 'What'
Shots – 'Ghost EP' (Dump Valve), which frieze says keeps the oriental flavour of 'What'

uncertainty: Neither the catalogue number nor the original format is confirmed: the Juno page is the reissue. The year 2004 comes from frieze only. A candidate for the 'sino-grime' coding (oriental chimes), but no source calls 'What' sinogrime by name. RADII says Kode9 'reportedly coined' 'Sinogrime' with his 2005 Sinogrime Minimix (https://radii.co/?p=17640).

title: Ghetto Kyote
label: White label
tracklist_note: Instrumental first; vocal versions followed in 2006, including one by Kano.

sound_descriptions.text: FACT: a lo-fi instrumental that sounds 'like they're lost in the snow'.
FACT: 'one of grime's greatest, most haunting ever moments'.

context.text: Credited to Treble Clef's crew Kamikaze; a Butterz reissue was planned but stalled.
Treble Clef's live version of the track became a cult YouTube hit.

relationships.other: DaVinChe-written version of 'Ghetto Kyote' (DaVinChe says he wrote the song but did not make the beat)

uncertainty: Added in place of DJ Davinche, for whom no 2002–06 release with a label could be verified. Treble Clef's area of London was not confirmed. FACT's 20 Best list credits it to 'Kamikaze / Treble Clef'. Kano is outside this batch, but the link is recorded only as a relationship.

title: Gladiator
producers: Alias (J Sweet and Pele, per FACT; not confirmed for this track)
label: Alias
tracklist_note: Companion anthem 'Warriors' is also named by FACT.

sound_descriptions.text: FACT groups it with grime's hard-edged instrumentals but gives no further sonic detail.

context.text: Listed in FACT's 20 best grime records as Alias, 'Gladiator', 2003, on the Alias label.
FACT names 'Gladiator' and 'Warriors' as Alias anthems and describes J Sweet and Pele as Alias's production side.
Included in Vice's all-time grime playlist (2012) and in Son Raw's Classic Grime Riddims mix.

uncertainty: This is the weakest-supported entry: only one source (FACT) gives the year and label, there is no usable sound description, and the producer credit is not confirmed for this track. Keep it as provisional or drop it if the register needs two independent sources.
